abstract: A photospheric horizontal velocity field was observed in an active region, NOAA 8375, which showed high H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> surge activities on 1998 November 6. From analyses of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> images, the photospheric horizontal velocity field, and the magnetic field in and around the active region, we found the following: (1) Meso-granular or supergranular photospheric horizontal motions were found to be suppressed in the active region where the magnetic filed strength was high. No systematic large-scale flows were found carrying the moving satellite spots with them. (2) Roots of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> surges were situated near a magnetic neutral line, where photospheric horizontal flow converged. Anti-polar magnetic fields on both sides of the neutral line were pushed together by the photospheric horizontal velocity field of meso-granular scales. Magnetic cancellation or magnetic reconnection in the chromospheric and/or photospheric layers at a magnetic neutral line accelerated by photospheric horizontal flows may be the origin of the observed H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> surge activities.

articleTitle: Orbital Period Analysis of Eclipsing Z Cam-Type Dwarf Nova EM Cygni: Evidence of Magnetic Braking and a Third Body
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Combining with our newest CCD times of light minimum of EM Cygni, all 45 available times of light minimum, including 7 data with large scatters, were compiled and an updated <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> analysis was made. The best-fit for the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> diagram of EM Cygni was a quadratic-plus-sinusoidal fit. The secular orbital period decrease rate (-2.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.3) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-11}\ $</tex>s s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> means that a magnetic braking effect in EM Cygni with a mass-loss rate caused by stellar wind, 2.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-10}\ M_{\odot}\ $</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, is needed for explaining the observed orbital period decrease. Moreover, for explaining the significant cyclical period change with a period of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>17.74 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.01 yr, shown in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> diagram, magnetic activity cycles and a light travel-time effect were considered in detail. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O-C$</tex> diagram of EM Cygni cannot totally rule out the possibility of multi-periodic modulation due to gaps present after 25000 cycles. Based on the hypothesis of a K-type third star in the literature, a light trave-time effect may be a more plausible explanation. However, the low orbital inclination of the third body (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ\!\!\!.$</tex>4) suggests that the hypothetic K-type third star may be captured by EM Cygni. But, by assuming the spectral contamination from a block of circumbinary material instead of a K-type third star, the third star may be a brown dwarf in the case of a coplanar orbit with a parent binary.

articleTitle: A Novel Jet Model: Magnetically Collimated, Radiation-Pressure Driven Jet
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Relativistic jets from compact objects are ubiquitous phenomena in the Unvierse, but their driving mechanism has been an enigmatic issue for several decades. Two basic models have been extensively discussed: magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) jets and radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) jets. Currently, the former is more widely accepted, since the magnetic field is expected to provide both acceleration and collimation mechanisms, whereas the radiation field cannot collimate the outflow. Here, we propose a new type of jets, radiation-magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) jets, based on our global RMHD simulation of luminous accretion flows onto a black hole shining above the Eddington luminosity. The RMHD jet can be accelerated up to relativistic speed by the radiation-pressure force and collimated by the Lorentz force of a magnetic tower structure inflated by toroidal magnetic field lines accumulated around the black hole, though the radiation energy greatly dominates over the magnetic energy. This magnetic tower is collimated by a geometrically thick accretion flow supported by a radiation-pressure force. This type of jet may explain relativistic jets from Galactic microquasars, appearing at high luminosity.

articleTitle: A New Set of Variables in the Three-Body Problem
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose a set of variables of the general three-body problem both for two-dimensional and three-dimensional cases. The variables are (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda, \theta, \Lambda, \Theta, k, \omega$</tex>), or equivalently (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda, \theta, L, \dot{I},k,\omega)$</tex> for the two-dimensional problem, and (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda, \theta, L, \dot{I}, k, \omega, \phi, \psi$</tex>) for the three-dimensional problem. Here, (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda, \theta$</tex>) and (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Lambda, \Theta)$</tex> specify the positions in the shape spheres in the configuration and momentum spaces, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k$</tex> is the virial ratio, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex> is the total angular momentum, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{I}$</tex> is the time derivative of the moment of inertia, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega, \phi$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\psi$</tex> are the Euler angles to bring the momentum triangle from the nominal position to a given position. This set of variables defines a shape space  of the three-body problem. This is also used as an initial-condition space. The initial condition of the so-called free-fall three-body problem is (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda, \theta, k =$</tex> 0, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L =$</tex> 0, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{I} =$</tex> 0, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega =$</tex> 0). We show that the hyper-surface <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{I} =$</tex> 0 is a global surface of section.

articleTitle: Time Variability of the Geocoronal Solar-Wind Charge Exchange in the Direction of the Celestial Equator
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the detection of a time variable OVII line emission in a deep 100 ks Suzaku X-ray Imaging Spectrometer spectrum of the galactic ridge X-ray emission. The observed line intensity is too strong (11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>2 line unit or photon cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>sr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>) to be emitted inside the heavily obscured galactic disk. It showed a factor of two time variation that showed a significant (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex>) correlation with the solar-wind O<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{7+}$</tex> ion flux. The high line intensity and good time correlation with the solar wind strongly suggests that it originated from geocoronal solar-wind charge-exchange emission. We discuss the X-ray line intensity while considering a line-of-sight direction and also theoretical distribution models of the neutral hydrogen and solar wind around Earth. Our results indicate that X-ray observations of geocoronal solar-wind charge-exchange emission can be used to constrain these models.

articleTitle: Spectral Index and Core-Dominance Parameter in Blazars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper, we discuss the relationship between the spectral index and the core-dominance parameter for blazars (BL Lacertae objects and flat spectrum radio quasars). To do so, we calculated the spectral indexes for 38 BL Lacertae objects using the preliminary data of the University of Michigan Radio Astronomy Observatory (UMRAO) with those for flat spectrum radio quasars from our previous paper (2008, PASJ, 60, 707). For the core-dominance parameters, we mainly calculated them from the flux densities given by Kovalev et al. (2005, AJ, 130, 2473). We have compiled a list of core-dominance parameters for some sources from the available literature. In this sense, we obtained a sample of 119 blazars (38 BL Lacertae objects and 81 flat spectrum radio quasars). From the relevant data, we found that the spectral index is associated with the core-dominance parameter, and tried to explain this association using a relativistic beaming model. In addition, we made a comparison of the properties of BL Lacertae objects and flat spectrum radio quasars. We concluded that the association between spectral index and core-dominance parameter is perhaps due to a relativistic beaming effect.

articleTitle: Milne–Eddington Solutions for Relativistic Spherical Flows
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Relativistic radiative transfer in a relativistic spherical flow is examined using a fully special relativistic treatment. Under the assumption of a constant flow speed, we obtain analytical solutions of radiative moment equations in the case of a constant comoving luminosity, and in the streaming limit. In the case of a constant comoving luminosity, in the non-relativistic regime the luminosity in the inertial frame is constant, whereas in the relativistic regime there appears a term proportional to the velocity and the optical depth. The spherical pressure in the relativistic regime is also enhanced compared with that in the non-relativistic regime. In the case of the streaming limit, we can also integrate moment equations analytically to obtain the luminosity and the spherical pressure in the inertial frame. In this case the inertial luminosity increases with the optical depth, but the comoving one reduces. On the other hand, the spherical pressure in the inertial frame, which is proportional to the optical depth in the non-relativistic regime, reduces as the flow speed increases. These properties are similar to the plane-parallel case, if the luminosity and the spherical pressure are exchanged by the flux and the usual pressure, respectively.

articleTitle: A Detailed Observational Study of Molecular Loops 1 and 2 in the Galactic Center
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Fukui et al. (2006, Science, 314, 106) discovered two huge molecular loops in the galactic center located at (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l, b$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq$</tex> (355<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>–359<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>, 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>–2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>) in a large velocity range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>180—40 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Following the discovery, we present detailed observational properties of the two loops based on NANTEN <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) datasets at 10 pc resolution, including a complete set of velocity channel distributions and comparisons with HI and dust emissions as well as with the other broad molecular features. We have found new features on smaller scales in the loops, including helical distributions in the loop tops and vertical spurs. The loops have counterparts of the HI gas, indicating that the loops include atomic gas. The IRAS far-infrared emission is also associated with the loops, and was used to derive an X-factor of 0.7 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.1) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{20}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> (K km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> to convert the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO intensity into the total molecular hydrogen column density. From the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO, HI, and dust datasets we estimated the total mass of loops 1 and 2 to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>1.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^6$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\odot$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>1.9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^6$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\odot$</tex>, respectively, where the HI mass corresponds to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>10%–20% of the total mass and the total kinetic energy of the two loops is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{52}\ $</tex>erg. An analysis of the kinematics of the loops yields that the loops are rotating at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>47 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> and expanding at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>141 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> at a radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>670 pc from the center. Fukui et al. (2006) presented a model that the loops are created by magnetic flotation due to the Parker instability with an estimated magnetic field strength of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>150<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>G. We present comparisons with the recent numerical simulations of the magnetized nuclear disk by Machida et al. (2009, PASJ, 61, 411) and Takahashi et al. (2009, PASJ, 61, 957), and show that the theoretical results are in good agreement with the observations. The helical distributions also suggest that some magnetic instability plays a role similarly to the solar helical features.

articleTitle: The AMANOGAWA-2SB Galactic Plane Survey I. Data on the Galactic Equator
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using a waveguide-type sideband-separating receiver (2SB receiver) on the Tokyo-NRO 60-cm telescope (renamed the AMANOGAWA telescope), we carried out simultaneous observations in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1) lines over the galactic plane <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l =$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>–245<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> along <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> with a 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$'\!\!.$</tex>75 grid. Using the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) data of Dame et al. (2001, ApJ, 547, 792), who used a beam size almost the same as ours, we show <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1) intensity ratios on the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v$</tex> map and the intensity correlations among the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1), and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) lines. As a result, a linear correlation between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) and a curved correlation between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1), as produced by most of the data, have been found. We investigated these correlations with simple radiative transfer equations to ascertain a number of restrictions on the physical quantities of molecular gas on a galactic scale.

articleTitle: Warm and Dense Molecular Gas in the N 159 Region: 12CO J = 4–3 and 13CO J = 3–2 Observations with NANTEN2 and ASTE
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: New <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 3–2 observations of the N 159 region, an active site of massive star formation in the Large Magellanic Cloud, have been made with the NANTEN2 and ASTE submillimeter telescopes, respectively. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3 distribution is separated into three clumps, each associated with N 159 W, N 159 E, and N 159 S. These new measurements toward the three clumps are used in coupled calculations of molecular rotational excitation and line radiation transfer, along with other transitions of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 3–2, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 7–6 as well as the isotope transitions of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 2–1, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 3–2, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 3–2 data were newly taken for the present work. The temperatures and densities were found to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>70&x2013;80 K and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> in N 159 W and N 159 E, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>30 K and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>1.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> in N 159 S. These results were compared with the star-formation activity based on data of young stellar clusters and HII regions as well as midinfrared emission obtained with the Spitzer MIPS. The N 159 E clump is associated with cluster(s) embedded, as observed at 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m by the Spitzer MIPS, and the derived high temperature, 80 K, is interpreted as being heated by these sources. The N 159 E clump is likely to be responsible for a dark lane in a large H II region by dust extinction. On the other hand, the N 159 W clump is associated with clusters embedded mainly toward the eastern edge of the clump only. These clusters show offsets of 20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{\prime\prime}$</tex>–40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{\prime\prime}$</tex> from the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3 peak, and are probably responsible for heating indicated by the derived high temperature, 70 K. The N 159 W clump exhibits no sign of star formation toward the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3 peak position and its western region that shows enhanced <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{4-3/1-0}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{3-2/1-0}$</tex> ratios. We therefore suggest that the N 159 W peak represents a pre-star-cluster core of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5} M_{\odot}$</tex> which deserves further detailed studies. The N 159 S clump shows little sign of star formation, as is consistent with the lower temperature, 30 K, and has a somewhat lower density than N 159 W and N 159 E. The N 159 S clump is also a candidate for future star formation.

articleTitle: Suzaku Discovery of a Hard X-Ray Tail in the Persistent Spectra from the Magnetar 1E 1547.0-5408 during its 2009 Activity
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The fastest-rotating magnetar 1E 1547.0-5408 was observed in broad-band X-rays with Suzaku for 33 ks on 2009 January 28–29, 7 d after the onset of its latest bursting activity. After removing burst events, the absorption-uncorrected 2–10 keV flux of the persistent emission was measured with the XIS as 5.7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-11} $</tex>erg cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, which is 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than was measured in 2006 and 2007 when the source was less active. This persistent emission was also detected significantly with the HXD in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> $</tex>10 keV up to at least <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>110 keV, with an even higher flux of 1.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-10} $</tex>erg cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> in 20–100 keV. The pulsation was detected at least up to 70 keV for a period of 2.072135<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.00005 s, with a deeper modulation than was measured in a fainter state. The phase-averaged 0.7–114 keV spectrum was reproduced by an absorbed blackbody emission with a temperature of 0.65<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.02 keV, plus a hard power-law with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>1.5. At a distance of 9 kpc, the bolometric luminosity of the blackbody and the 2–100 keV luminosity of the hard power-law are estimated to be (6.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>1.2) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{35} $</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> and 1.9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{36} $</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, respectively, while the blackbody radius becomes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>5 km. Although the source has not been detected significantly in hard X-rays during the past fainter states, a comparison of the present and past spectra at energies below 10 keV suggests that the hard component is more enhanced than the soft X-ray component during the period of persistent activity.

articleTitle: Temperature and Density in the Foot Points of the Molecular Loops in the Galactic Center; Analysis of Multi-J Transitions of 12CO (J = 1–0, 3–2, 4–3, 7–6), 13CO (J = 1–0), and C18O (J = 1–0)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Fukui et al. (2006, Science, 314, 106) discovered two molecular loops in the Galactic center, and argued that the foot points of the molecular loops, two bright spots at both loop ends, represent gas accumulated by the falling motion along the loops, subsequent to magnetic flotation by the Parker instability. We have carried out sensitive CO observations of the foot points toward <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l =$</tex> 356<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex> at a few pc resolution in the six rotational transitions of CO: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0, 3–2, 4–3, 7–6), <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0), and C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{18}$</tex>O (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0). A high-resolution image of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 3–2) has revealed the detailed distribution of the high-excitation gas, including U shapes, the outer boundary of which shows sharp intensity jumps accompanying strong velocity gradients. An analysis of the multi-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex> CO transitions shows that the temperature is in the range from 30 to 100 K and the density is around 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{3}$</tex>–10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{4} $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>, confirming that the foot points have high temperature and density, although there is no prominent radiative heating source, such as high-mass stars in or around the loops. We argue that the high temperature is likely due to shock heating under the C-shock condition caused by magnetic flotation. We made a comparison of the gas distribution with theoretical numerical simulations, and note that the U shape is consistent with numerical simulations. We also find that the region of highest temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>100 K or higher inside the U shape corresponds to the spur having an upward flow, additionally heated up either by magnetic reconnection or bouncing in the interaction with the narrow neck at the bottom of the U shape. We note that these new findings further reinforce the magnetic floatation interpretation.

articleTitle: Excitation of Trapped g-Mode Oscillations in Warped Disks around Black Holes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to study the origin of high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations observed in X-ray binaries, Kato (2004) suggested a resonant excitation mechanism of disk oscillations in deformed disks. In this paper, we investigate numerically, following his formulation, whether trapped g-mode oscillations in a warped disk, where the warp amplitude varies with the radius, can be excited by this mechanism. For simplicity, we adopt Newtonian hydrodynamic equations with relativistic expressions for the characteristic frequencies of disks. We also assume that the accretion disk is isothermal. We find that the fundamental modes of trapped g-mode oscillations with eigenfrequencies close to the maximum of epicyclic frequency are excited. The intermediate oscillations found are isolated in a narrow region around the resonance radius. After varying some parameters, we find that the growth rate increases as the warp amplitude or the black-hole spin parameter increases, while it decreases as the sound speed increases.

articleTitle: Mass Estimation of Merging Galaxy Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigate the impact of mergers on the mass estimation of galaxy clusters using <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body + hydrodynamical simulation data. We estimate the virial mass from these data and compare it with the real mass. When a smaller subcluster’s mass is larger than a quarter of that of the larger one, the virial mass can be larger than twice the real mass. The results strongly depend on the observational directions, because of an anisotropic velocity distribution of the member galaxies. We have also made X-ray surface brightness and spectroscopic-like temperature maps from the simulation data. The mass profile is estimated from these data on the assumption of hydrostatic equilibrium. In general, a mass estimation with X-ray data gives us better results than a virial mass estimation. The dependence upon observational directions is weaker than in the case of a virial mass estimation. When the system is observed along the collision axis, the projected mass tends to be underestimated. This fact should be noted, especially when the virial and/or X-ray mass is compared with gravitational lensing results.

articleTitle: Sensitivity Analysis of Optical Systems in Radio Telescopes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have demonstrated an approach to predict the overall efficiency and system noise regarding optical systems in radio telescopes, based on a systematic evaluation of both the optical propagation efficiency through all optical components, from the receiver horn to the main reflector, and of their noise contributions. The analysis employs several conventional techniques, including the principle of multimode Gaussian optics and calculations of losses associated with optical components. A detailed analysis was performed for cases of ALMA band 4 (125–163 GHz) and 8 (385–500 GHz). The analysis predicts a reasonable efficiency of 0.75–0.76 (0.57–0.62) and a system noise of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>70 K (300–400 K) for band 4 (band 8). The calculated efficiency of the band 4 optics was found to be consistent with the efficiency measured by astronomical observations with the ALMA/ACA 12-m antenna. In addition to a confirmation that the bands 4 and 8 optics were designed to maximize the overall efficiency, the analysis for the bands 4 and 8 frequency ranges also confirmed that there is no difference in the optimum edge levels at the subreflector between the two different ways of maximization, i.e., toward the overall efficiency or the sensitivity, which is defined by the ratio of the overall efficiency over the sum of noises generated from all possible sources. We also applied a sensitivity analysis to the band 1 frequency case, and revealed a slight, but clear, difference in the optimum edge levels between the sensitivity and the efficiency (difference is 1–2 dB). This corresponds to a sensitivity loss of 1% if we optimize the optics to maximize the efficiency.

articleTitle: Distance to G14.33–0.64 in the Sagittarius Spiral Arm: H2O Maser Trigonometric Parallax with VERA
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on trigonometric parallax measurements for the Galactic star-forming region G14.33-0.64 toward the Sagittarius spiral arm. We conducted multi-epoch phase-referencing observations of an H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser source in G14.33-0.64 with the Japanese VLBI array VERA. We successfully detected a parallax of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pi =$</tex> 0.893<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.101 mas, corresponding to a source distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d =$</tex> 1.12<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>0.13 kpc, which is less than half of the kinematic distance for G14.33-0.64. Our new distance measurement demonstrates that the Sagittarius arm lies at a closer distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1 kpc, instead of the previously assumed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2–3 kpc from the kinematic distances. The previously suggested deviation of the Sagittarius arm toward the Galactic center from the symmetrically fitted model (Taylor & Cordes 1993, ApJ, 411, 674) is likely due to large errors of the kinematic distances at low galactic longitudes. G14.33-0.64 most likely traces the near side of the Sagittarius arm. We attempted to fit the pitch angle of the arm with other parallax measurements along the arm, which yielded two possible pitch angles of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i =$</tex> 34°.7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>2°.7 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i =$</tex> 11.D2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \pm $</tex>10.D5. Our proper-motion measurements suggest that G14.33-0.64 has no significant peculiar motion relative to the differential rotation of the Galaxy (assumed to be in a circular orbit), indicating that the source motion is in good agreement with the Galactic rotation.

articleTitle: X-Ray Temperature and Mass Measurements to the Virial Radius of Abell 1413 with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present X-ray observations of the northern outskirts of the relaxed galaxy cluster A 1413 with Suzaku, whose XIS instrument has the low intrinsic background needed to make measurements of these low surface brightness regions. We excised 15 point sources superimposed on the image above a flux of 1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-14}$</tex>erg cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2} $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> (2–10 keV) using XMM-Newton and Suzaku images of the cluster. We quantified all known systematic errors as part of our analysis, and showed that our statistical errors encompass them for the most part. Our results extend previous measurements with Chandra and XMM-Newton, and show a significant temperature drop to about 3 keV at the virial radius, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{200}$</tex>. Our entropy profile in the outer region (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> $</tex>0.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{200}$</tex>) joins smoothly onto that of XMM-Newton, and shows a flatter slope compared with simple models, similar to a few other clusters observed at the virial radius. The integrated mass of the cluster at the virial radius is approximately 7.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14} M_{\odot}$</tex>, and varies by about 30%, depending on the particular method used to measure it.

articleTitle: Fibre Multi-Object Spectrograph (FMOS) for the Subaru Telescope
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Fibre Multi-Object Spectrograph (FMOS) is the first near-infrared instrument with a wide field of view capable of acquiring spectra simultaneously from up to 400 objects. It has been developed as a common-use instrument for the F<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex>2 prime-focus of the Subaru Telescope. The field coverage of 30<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> diameter is achieved using a new 3-element corrector optimized in the near-infrared (0.9–1.8<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m) wavelength range. Due to limited space at the prime-focus, we have had to develop a novel fibre positioner, called “Echidna”, together with two OH-airglow suppressed spectrographs. FMOS consists of three subsystems: the prime focus unit for IR, the fibre positioning system/connector units, and the two spectrographs. After full systems integration, FMOS was installed on the telescope in late 2007. Many aspects of the performance were checked through various test and engineering observations. In this paper, we present the optical and mechanical components of FMOS, and show the results of our on-sky engineering observations to date.

articleTitle: LoCuSS: Subaru Weak Lensing Study of 30 Galaxy Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We use high-quality Subaru/Suprime-Cam imaging data to conduct a detailed weak lensing study of the distribution of dark matter in a sample of 30 X-ray luminous galaxy clusters at 0.15 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\le z \le$</tex> 0.3. A weak lensing signal is detected at high statistical significance in each cluster, the total signal-to-noise ratio of the detections ranging from 5 to 13. Comparing spherical models to the tangential distortion profiles of the clusters individually, we are unable to discriminate statistically between a singular isothermal sphere (SIS) and Navarro, Frenk, and White (NFW) models. However, when the tangential distortion profiles are combined and then models are fitted to the stacked profile, the SIS model is rejected at 6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex> and 11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex>, respectively, for low (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir}<$</tex> 6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$</tex>) and high (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir} > $</tex> 6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$</tex>) mass bins. We also used individual cluster NFW model fits to investigate the relationship between the cluster mass and the concentration, finding that the concentration (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm vir}$</tex>) decreases with increasing cluster mass (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir}$</tex>). The best-fit <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm vir}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir}$</tex> relation is: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm vir}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir}$</tex>) = 8.75<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+4.13}_{-2.89} \times$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir}/$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14}\ h^{-1}\ M_\odot$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-\alpha}$</tex> with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha \approx$</tex> 0.40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.19: i.e., a non-zero slope is detected at 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex> significance. This relation gives a concentration of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm vir} =$</tex> 3.48<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+1.65}_{-1.15}$</tex> for clusters with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm vir} =$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{15}\ h^{-1}M_\odot$</tex>, which is inconsistent at 4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex> significance with the values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm vir} \sim$</tex> 10 reported for strong-lensing-selected clusters. We have found that the measurement error on the cluster mass is smaller at higher over-densities, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta \simeq$</tex> 500–2000, than at the virial over-density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta_{\rm vir} \simeq$</tex> 110; typical fractional errors at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta \simeq$</tex> 500–2000 are improved to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\Delta$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/M_{\Delta } \simeq$</tex> 0.1–0.2 compared with 0.2–0.3 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta_{\rm vir}$</tex>. Furthermore, comparing the 3D spherical mass with the 2D cylinder mass, obtained from the aperture mass method at a given aperture radius, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\theta_\Delta$</tex>, reveals <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm 2D}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< \theta_{\Delta}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/M_{\rm 3D}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< r_\Delta = D_{\rm l}\theta_{\Delta}$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq$</tex> 1.46 and 1.32 for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta =$</tex> 500 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta_{\rm vir}$</tex>, respectively. The amplitude of this offset agrees well with that predicted by integrating an NFW model of cluster-scale halos along the line-of-sight.

articleTitle: The Mass Distribution of SDSS J1004+4112 Revisited
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a strong lens analysis of SDSS J1004+4112, a unique quasar lens produced by a massive cluster of galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z =$</tex> 0.68, using newly developed software for gravitational lensing. We find that our parametric mass model well reproduces all observations, including the positions of quasar images as well as those of multiply imaged galaxies with measured spectroscopic redshifts, time delays between quasar images, and the positions of faint central images. The predicted large total magnification of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu \sim$</tex> 70 suggests that the lens system is indeed a useful site for studying the fine structure of a distant quasar and its host galaxy. The dark halo component is found to be unimodal, centered on the brightest cluster galaxy and the Chandra X-ray surface brightness profile. In addition, the orientation of the halo component is quite consistent with those of the brightest cluster galaxy and member galaxy distribution, implying that the lensing cluster is a relaxed system. The radial profile of the best-fit mass model is in good agreement with a mass profile inferred from the X-ray observation. While the inner radial slope of the dark halo component is consistent with being -1, a clear dependence of the predicted A–D time delay on the slope indicates that an additional time-delay measurement will improve constraints on the mass model.

articleTitle: Oxygen and Neon Abundances of B-Type Stars in Comparison with the Sun
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: To revisit the long-standing problem of a possible inconsistency concerning the oxygen composition in the current Galactic gas and in the solar atmosphere (i.e., the former being appreciably lower by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.3 dex), apparently contradicting the Galactic chemical evolution, we carried out oxygen abundance determinations for 64 mid- through late-B stars by using the O I 6156–8 lines while taking into account the non-LTE effect, and compared them with the solar O abundance established in the same manner. The resulting mean oxygen abundance was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\langle A^{\rm O} \rangle =$</tex> 8.71 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.06), which means that [O<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex>H] (star <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex> Sun differential abundance) is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim-$</tex>0.1, the difference being less significant than previously thought. Moreover, since the 3D correction may further reduce the reference solar oxygen abundance (8.81) by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.1 dex, we conclude that the photospheric O abundances of these B stars are almost the same as that of the Sun. We also determined the non-LTE abundances of neon for sample B stars from Ne I 6143/6163 lines to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\langle A^{\rm Ne} \rangle =$</tex> 8.02 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex> 0.09), leading to an Ne-to-O ratio of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.2, consistent with recent studies. This excludes the possibility of a considerably high Ne<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/$</tex>O ratio once proposed as a solution to the confronted solar model problem.

articleTitle: Suzaku Wide-Band X-Ray Observation of the Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 Galaxy Ton S180
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We observed the luminous narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Ton S180 with Suzaku, and obtained its wide-band (0.25–55 keV) X-ray spectra for the first time. The spectra were modeled with three components: a power-law component, a reflection from a highly ionized disk component, and an extra soft component either of a disk blackbody or a cutoff power-law. The reflection component accounts for the broad iron K line centered at 6.7 keV, and some fraction of the soft X-ray excess, including the OVIII line emission. The latter two components contribute comparably to the soft X-ray excess. When we adopt the disk blackbody model as the extra soft component, the disk inner radius temperature is 75 eV, much smaller than previously considered. This component is almost consistent with that expected for the slim-disk model assuming edge-on geometry. Hard X-ray emission above 15 keV was marginally detected. To account for the hard X-ray spectrum, we introduced Compton-thick partial absorbers. The absence of the neutral iron K line requires that those absorbers must be preferentially located along the line of sight. Fractional variability has little energy dependence below 10 keV, and is explained with a model in which the covering fraction of the Compton-thick absorber alters the observed flux.

articleTitle: FAST: A Fully Asynchronous Split Time-Integrator for a Self-Gravitating Fluid
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We describe a new algorithm for the integration of self-gravitating fluid systems using SPH method. We split the Hamiltonian of a self-gravitating fluid system into the gravitational potential and others (kinetic and internal energies), and used different time-steps for their integrations. The time integration was done in the way similar to that used in the mixed-variable or multiple stepsize symplectic schemes. We performed three test calculations. The first test was spherical collapse, and the second test was an explosion. As the third test, we also performed a realistic test, in which the initial model was taken from a simulation of merging galaxies. In all test calculations, we found that the number of time-steps for gravitational interaction were reduced by nearly an order of magnitude when we adopted our integration method. In the case of the realistic test, in which the dark-matter potential dominates the total system, the total calculation time was significantly reduced. The simulation results were almost the same as those of simulations with the ordinary individual time-step method. Our new method has achieved good performance without sacrificing the accuracy of the time integration.

articleTitle: Subaru Near-Infrared Imaging of Herbig Ae Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report results of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H$</tex>-band (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda =$</tex> 1.65<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu$</tex>m) imaging observations of young intermediate-mass stars using the Subaru 8.2-m Telescope with the adaptive optics AO36 and the infrared coronagraph CIAO. The targets consist of 16 Herbig Ae/Be stars (15 Herbig Ae stars and one Herbig Be star) and four additional main-sequence stars with infrared excesses. Five protoplanetary disks have been spatially resolved around the Herbig Ae stars with ages of 2–8 Myr. The resolved disks have outer radii of several 100 AU, and their surface brightnesses range from 10 mag arcsec<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> to 18 mag arcsec<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>. The images reveal various morphologies in optically thick disks: spiral arms around AB Aur, a banana-split structure with an outer arm for HD 142527, a compact circumprimary disk of HD 150193, a faint discontinuous ring around HD 163296, and an unstructured face-on disk of HD 169142. The detection of an optically thick disk in scattered light implies that it is vertically flared, and intercepts stellar light at least in the outer region where those images were obtained. However, the surface brightness distribution, the resolved structure, and other observational characteristics suggest that the disks are unlikely to be continuously flared young disks with small grains well mixed with gas. The detection rate and the disk brightness do not correlate with the stellar age and the disk mass, but there is a tendency that the brightest disks are still surrounded by long-lived envelopes (AB Aur, HD 100546, HD 142527). The significant diversity of the disk structure can be attributed to the multiplicity and the initial condition of the local star-forming environments. The detections of companion candidates around our targeted stars are also reported.

articleTitle: Mass-Loss Timescale of Star Clusters in an External Tidal Field. II. Effect of Mass Profile of Parent Galaxy
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigate the long-term dynamical evolution of star clusters in a steady tidal field produced by its parent galaxy. In this paper, we focus on the influence of the mass profile of the parent galaxy. Previous studies were done with simplification, where the parent galaxy was expressed by the point mass. We express different mass profiles of the parent galaxy by the tidal fields in which the ratios of the epicyclic frequency, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\kappa$</tex>, to the angular velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega$</tex>, are different. We compare the mass-loss timescale of star clusters whose tidal radii are identical, but in parent galaxies with different mass profiles, by means of orbits calculations in fixed cluster potential and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body simulations. In this situation, a cluster rotates around the parent galaxy more rapidly, since the parent galaxy has a shallower mass profile. We found that the mass-loss timescale increase by 20% and 50% for the cases that the mass-density profiles of the parent galaxies are proportional to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R^{-2}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R^{-1.5}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex> is the distance from the galaxy center, compared to the point-mass case, in a moderately strong tidal field. Counterintuitively, a cluster that rotates around the parent galaxy more rapidly has a longer lifetime. The increase of the lifetime is due to the fact that the fraction occupied by a regular-like orbit increases in a shallower profile. Finally, we derive an evaluation formula for the mass-loss timescale of clusters. Our formula can explain a property of the population of the observed galactic globular clusters, that their half-mass radii become smaller as their distances from the galactic center become smaller.

articleTitle: Variation of Molecular Gas Properties Across the Spiral Arms in IC 342: Large-Scale 13CO (1–0) Emission
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (1–0) mapping survey of the nearby galaxy IC 342 carried out with the Nobeyama 45 m radio telescope. The map covers a 320<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime} \times$</tex> 320<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime}$</tex> region, including its center, bar, and most of one of the spiral arms. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (1–0) data were compared with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (1–0), H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\rm s}$</tex>-band images to investigate spatial relations among molecular clouds, star-forming regions, and the stellar potential. The line ratio between both CO lines, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex>[<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (1–0)]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/I$</tex>[<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (1–0)] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\equiv R_{13/12}$</tex>, was also derived to investigate the variation of molecular gas properties. The mean value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> in the center of IC 342 is low (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.01) compared to the disk region (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.01). While <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> in the central region is rather uniform, significant variations of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> were found in the spiral arms; that is, while it is low (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.1) at both ends of the bar and at the giant molecular cloud association (GMA) found in the spiral arm, it is high (0.14–0.20) downstream from the low <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> region. The low- and high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> regions in the disk correspond to the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO peak and star-forming regions, respectively. The low <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> in the galactic center is likely due to the higher gas temperature in the starburst region. The most probable explanation of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> variation in the disk is that a low <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> in the GMA and the ends of the bar reflects an increased fraction of the diffuse molecular component, which has a low column density and low volume density. Around the GMA and the north end of the bar, not only are the star-forming regions downstream from the CO distributions, but <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{13/12}$</tex> is also higher downstream, implying the presence of gas compression and ionized/molecular gas spatial offsets, as predicted by density wave models.

articleTitle: First R and I Lights and Their Photometric Analyses of GSC 02393–00680
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We obtained complete <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex> light curves of GSC 02393-00680 in 2008 and analyzed them with the 2003 version of the W–D code. It has been shown that GSC 02393-00680 is a W-type shallow contact binary system with a high mass ratio, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$q =$</tex> 1.600, and a degree of contact factor, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f =$</tex> 5.0% (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>1.3%). It will be a good example to check up on the TRO theory. A period investigation based on all available data suggests that the system has a small-amplitude period oscillation (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_3 =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$.^{\rm d}$</tex>0030; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_3 =$</tex> 1.92 years). This may indicate that it has a moderate-mass close third body, which is similar to XY Leo.

articleTitle: Comparison of AGN and Nuclear Starburst Activity in Seyfert 1 and 2 Galaxies over a Wide Luminosity Range Based on Near-Infrared 2–4μm Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present near-infrared <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>- (1.9–2.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>- (2.8–4.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m) band spectroscopy of 22 Seyfert nuclei. We used two methods to investigate the presence of nuclear starbursts: (1) the Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) emission feature at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\rm rest}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 3.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m in the rest frame of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>-band spectrum (a starburst indicator) and (2) the CO absorption feature at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\rm rest}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$=$</tex> 2.3–2.4<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m in the rest frame of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>-band spectrum, originating in the CO molecule. We clearly detected the 3.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m PAH emission features in five objects and the CO absorption features in 17 objects. Seyfert 2 galaxies tend to show bluer <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex> colors compared with Seyfert 1 galaxies. We interpret the discrepancy as resulting from the relative strength of stellar emission because AGN emission is affected by dust extinction. The 3.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m PAH emission luminosity (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm 3.3PAH}$</tex>) distributions for the Seyfert 1s and Seyfert 2s are very similar when normalized to the AGN power. The star-formation rates estimated from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm 3.3PAH}$</tex> could be large enough to inflate the dusty torus by a supernova explosion. We find that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm 3.3PAH}$</tex> positively correlates with the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-band luminosity with small aperture over a wide AGN luminosity range, and is independent of the physical area we probed. The results suggest that the nuclear region has a concentration of star formation and it would control the AGN activity.

articleTitle: Testing the Atacama Compact Array Phase-Correction Scheme Using the Submillimeter Array
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted observational tests of a phase-correction scheme for the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter and submillimeter Array (ALMA) using the Submillimeter Array (SMA) on Mauna Kea in Hawaii. Interferometers at millimeter and submillimeter waves are highly affected by refraction induced by water vapor in the troposphere, which results in phase fluctuations. The ACA is planning to compensate for the atmospheric phase fluctuation using phase information of the outermost antennas with interpolating into the inner antennas by creating a phase screen. The interpolation and extrapolation phase-correction schemes using phase screens have been tested by the SMA to study how effective they are. We produce a plane of wavefront (phase screen) from the phase information of three antennas for each integration, and this phase screen is used for interpolating the phase of the inner antenna and extrapolating that of the outer one.
