The interpolation scheme apparently obtains improved results, suggesting that the ACA phase-correction scheme works well. On the other hand, the extrapolation one often does not improve the results. After extrapolation, unexpectedly large phase fluctuations occur in the phases of the antennas at a distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>140 m away from the center of the three reference antennas. The directions of these antennas are almost perpendicular to that of the wind, suggesting that the phase fluctuations can be well explained by the frozen phase screen in the atmosphere.

articleTitle: Suzaku X-Ray and Optical Spectroscopic Observations of SS 433 in the 2006 April Multiwavelength Campaign
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on results of the 2006 April multiwavelength campaign of SS 433, focusing on X-ray data observed with Suzaku at two orbital phases (in- and out-of-eclipse phases) and on simultaneous optical spectroscopic observations. Analyzing the FeXXV K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> lines originating from the jets, we detected a rapid variability of the Doppler shifts, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dz/dt \approx$</tex> 0.019/0.33d<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, which is larger than those expected from the precession and/or nodding motion. This phenomenon probably corresponds to “jitter” motions observed for the first time in X-rays, for which significant variabilities in both the jet angle and the intrinsic speed are required. From time lags between optical Doppler curves and X-ray ones, we estimated a distance between the optical jets and the base to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>(3-4) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{14}$</tex>cm. Based on the radiatively cooling jet model, we determined that the innermost temperatures of the jets are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_0 =$</tex> 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>2keV for the out-of-eclipse phase and 16<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>3keV for the in-eclipse (the average of the blue and red jets) from the line intensity ratio of FeXXV K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> and FeXXVI K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>. While the broad-band-continuum spectra over the 5-40keV band in eclipse is consistent with a multitemperature-bremsstrahlung emission expected from the jets and its reflection component from cold matter, the out-of-eclipse spectrum is harder than the jet emission with the base temperature determined above, implying the presence of an additional hard component.

articleTitle: SiO and H2O Maser Observations of Red Supergiants in Star Clusters Embedded in the Galactic Disk
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of radio observations of red supergiants in a star cluster, Stephenson (1990, AJ, 99, 1867)’s #2, and of candidates for red supergiants in three star clusters, Mercer et al. (2005, ApJ, 635, 560)’s #4, #8, and #13, in the SiO and H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser lines. The Stephenson’s #2 cluster and nearby aggregation at the southwest contain more than 15 red supergiants. We detected one red supergiant at the center of Stephenson’s #2 and three in a southwest aggregation in the SiO maser line; three out of these four were also detected in the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser line. The average radial velocity of the four detected objects is 97 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, giving a kinematic distance of 5.5 kpc, which locates this cluster near the base of the Scutum–Crux spiral arm. We also detected six SiO emitting objects associated with other star clusters. In addition, mapping observations in the CO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0 line toward these clusters revealed that an appreciable amount of molecular gas still remains around the Stephenson’s #2 cluster in contrast to the prototypical red-supergiant cluster, Bica et al. (2003, A&A, 404, 223)’s #122. This indicates that the time scale of gas expulsion differs considerably in individual clusters.

Author Keywords: open clusters and associations: individual (Mercer et al.’s #4, #8, #13; Stephenson’s #2)

articleTitle: Absolute Dimensions and Apsidal Motion of the Young Detached System LT Canis Majoris
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: New high-resolution spectra of the short-period (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P \sim$</tex> 1.76 days) young detached binary LT CMa are reported for the first time. By combining the results from an analysis of new radial-velocity curves and published light curves, we determine values for the masses, radii, and temperatures as follows: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm 1} =$</tex> 5.59 (0.20)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}, R_{\rm 1} =$</tex> 3.56 (0.07)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ R_{\odot}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff1} =$</tex> 17000 (500) K for the primary and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm 2} =$</tex> 3.36 (0.14)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ M_{\odot}, R_{\rm 2} =$</tex> 2.04 (0.05)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ R_{\odot}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff2} =$</tex> 13140 (800) K for the secondary. Static absorbtion features apart from those coming from the close binary components were detected in the several spectral regions. If these absorbtion features are from a third star, as the light-curve solutions support, its radial velocity is measured to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$RV_{\rm 3} =$</tex> 70 (8) km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The orbit of the binary system has been proved to be eccentric (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$e =$</tex> 0.059) and thus apsidal motion exists. The estimated linear advance in longitude of periastron corresponds to an apsidal motion of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U =$</tex> 69<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>5 yr for the system. The average internal structure constant, log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k_{\rm 2,obs} = -$</tex>2.53 of LT CMa, is found to be smaller than its theoretical value of log <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k_{\rm 2,theo} = -$</tex>2.22, suggesting that the stars would have a more central concentration in mass. The photometric distance of LT CMa (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$d =$</tex> 535<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>45 pc) is found to be much smaller than the distance of the CMa OB1 association (1150 pc), which rules out membership. A comparison with current stellar evolution models for solar metallicity indicates that LT CMa (35 Myr) is much older than the CMa OB1 association (3 Myr), confirming that LT CMa is not a member of CMa OB1. Kinematical and dynamical analyses indicate that LT CMa is orbiting the Galaxy in a circular orbit, and belongs to the young thin-disk population.

articleTitle: Stellar Parameters and Abundance Analysis of 58 Late G Giants
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present stellar atmospheric parameters, and kinematic parameters for a part of Xinglong Planet Search Program sample – 58 late G-type giants, obtained at Okayama Astrophysical Observatory. Additionally, we determined the chemical abundances, especially for the elements C, O, and Na. The metallicity distribution of our sample ranges covered from -0.6 to 0.2 in [Fe/H], which supports the previous results, suggesting a lack of super metal-rich giants with [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> +$</tex>0.2. The abundance of C is depleted by 0.13 dex, and [Na/Fe] shows an overabundance of 0.1 dex compared to a dwarf with the same spectral type, while the O abundance was not altered after the first dredge up. These results are consistent with theoretical predictions of stellar evolution. The behaviors of Si, Ca, Ti, Cr, Ni, Mn, ScII, YII, and CeII in our giants follow the same trends as in dwarfs.

articleTitle: Orbital Period Changes and Their Explanations in Two Algol Binaries: WY Per and RW Leo
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: WY Per and RW Leo are two Algol-type binaries. Based on our new CCD observations and the almost century-long historical record of the times of primary eclipses for WY Per and RW Leo, the orbital period changes and their explanations were reanalyzed and rediscussed in detail. It has been found that the orbital period of WY Per shows a cyclic oscillation with a period of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{3} =$</tex> 71.5 yr and a semiamplitude of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{3} =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}\!\!\!.$</tex>0739. The period variation can be interpreted by the light-travel time effect (LTTE) via the presence of a third body in an eccentric orbit with an eccentricity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$e_{3} \simeq$</tex> 0.602 in the system. For RW Leo, its orbital period shows complex variations. Two cyclic variations (i.e., <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{3} =$</tex> 77.8 yr and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{3} =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}\!\!\!.$</tex>033, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{4} =$</tex> 39.1 yr and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{4} =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}\!\!\!.$</tex>022) were discovered. The cyclic variations of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$P_{3} =$</tex> 77.8 yr and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{3} =$</tex> 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\rm d}\!\!\!.$</tex>033 can be attributed to the LTTE via the presence of a third body in an eccentric orbit with an eccentricity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$e_{3} \simeq$</tex> 0.732.

articleTitle: SiO Maser Survey off the Galactic Plane: A Signature of Streaming Motion
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A group of Mira variables in the solar neighborhood shows unusual spatial motion in the Galaxy. To study this motion on a much larger scale in the Galaxy, we newly surveyed 134 evolved stars off the Galactic plane by SiO maser lines, obtaining accurate radial velocities of 84 detected stars. Together with the past data of SiO maser sources, we analyzed the radial-velocity data of a large sample of sources distributed in a distance range of about 0.3–6 kpc in the first Galactic quadrant. At Galactic longitudes between 20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> and 40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>, we found a group of stars with large negative radial velocities, which deviate by more than 100 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> from the Galactic rotation. We show that these deviant motions of maser stars are created by periodic gravitational perturbation of the Bulge bar, and that the effect appears most strongly at radii between corotation and outer Lindblad resonances. The resonance effect can explain the displacement of positions from the Galactic plane as well.

articleTitle: Radiative Spectra from Disk Corona and Inner Hot Flow in Black-Hole X-Ray Binaries
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: To understand the origin of hard X-ray emissions from black-hole X-ray binaries during their low/hard states, we calculate the X-ray spectra of black-hole accretion flow for the following three configurations of hot and cool media: (a) an inner hot-flow and a cool outer disk (inner hot-flow model), (b) a cool disk sandwiched by disk coronae (disk-corona model), and (c) a combination of those two (hybrid model). The basic features we require for successful models are (i) significant hard X-ray emission whose luminosity exceeds that of soft X-rays, (ii) high hard X-ray luminosities in the range of (0.4–30) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{37}$</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and (iii) the existence of two power-law components in the hard X-ray band with photon indices of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm s} \sim$</tex> 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> \Gamma_{\rm h}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm s}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm h}$</tex> are the photon indices of the softer (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 10 keV) and harder (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>10 keV) power-law components, respectively. The contributions by non-thermal electrons or time-dependent evolution are not considered. We find that Models (a) and (b) can be ruled out, since the spectra are always dominated by the soft component, and since only one power-law component, at most, can be reproduced. Only Model (c) can account for sufficiently strong hard X-ray emissions, as well as the existence of the two power-law components, for a large ratio of the accretion rate in the corona to that in the thin disk. The outer-disk corona (where the Compton <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y$</tex>-parameter is smaller, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y <$</tex> 1) produces the softer power-law component with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm s} \sim$</tex> 2, whereas the inner hot-flow (where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$y >rsim$</tex> 1) generates the harder component with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm h} < $</tex> 2. This model can also account for the observed relationship between the photon index and the reflection fraction.

articleTitle: Solar-Type Magnetic Reconnection Model for Magnetar Giant Flares
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a theoretical model describing magnetar giant flares on the basis of solar flare/coronal mass ejection theory. In our model, preflare activity plays a crucial role in driving evaporating flows and supplying baryonic matter to the magnetosphere. Loaded baryonic matter, which is called “prominence”, is then gradually uplifted via crustal cracking while maintaining a quasi-force-free equilibrium of the magnetosphere. Finally, the prominence is erupted by a magnetic pressure force due to the loss of equilibrium triggered by explosive magnetic reconnection. A giant flare should be induced as a final outcome of prominence eruption accompanied by large-scale field reconfigurations. An essential difference between the solar flare and the magnetar flare is the control process of their evolutionary dynamics. The flaring activity on magnetars is mainly controlled by the radiative process, unlike a solar flare governed by electron conduction. It is full of suggestion that our model accounts for the physical properties of an extraordinary giant flare observed on 2004 December 27 from SGR 1806-20, including the source of baryonic matter loaded in the expanding ejecta observed after the giant burst.

articleTitle: A Catalog of Suzaku/WAM Hard X-Ray Solar Flares
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We developed a catalog of solar flares in the hard X-ray band observed with the Wide-band All-sky Monitor (WAM) onboard the Suzaku satellite between 2005 July and 2009 November. During this period, 105 solar flares (GOES class X: 13, M: 29, C: 47, B: 16) were detected with WAM, including 10% of GOES-class C events reported during the same period. The observed photon flux ranged between 9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-5}$</tex> and 9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>photons s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>keV<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex> at 100 keV. The averaged hard X-ray spectrum for each solar flare was evaluated for 70 of the 105 events, and 43 of them were well fitted with a single power-law model with a photon index ranging between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>7 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>3. We observed a weak trend where events with longer durations exhibited harder spectral slopes.

articleTitle: NANTEN Survey of Molecular Clouds toward the Galactic Center; Association of Compact Astronomical Objects
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to better understand molecular clouds and their properties toward the Galactic center region, we have analyzed the NANTEN database of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) to search for associations with candidates for young high-mass star-forming regions, such as IRAS point sources, radio continuum sources, recombination line sources, maser line sources, and other molecular line sources. We have also compared the data with TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray sources. The analyzed region covers -12<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ} \leq l \leq$</tex> 12<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> and -1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\leq b \leq$</tex> 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>5 for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO, and -6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ} \leq l \leq$</tex> 8<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> and -1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ} \leq b \leq$</tex> 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO. As a result, we identified 167 IRAS point sources, 73 recombination line sources, 58 maser sources, 107 radio continuum sources, and 77 molecular line sources associated with 169 positions with the CO emission. The associations among the objects with known velocity are fairly certain (68%), while those with only positional coincidence are less reliable (32%). We present a catalog of these CO clouds in a form useful for future follow-up studies. As specific examples of usage of the catalog, we highlight three outstanding regions of active star formation: W 28, W 30, and W 31. In particular, we have discovered that the W 30 region shows a striking correlation between the extended TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source and the molecular gas. This is a second case of such a good correlation identified from the NANTEN dataset subsequent to W 28 (Aharonian et al. 2008, A&A, 481, 401). We suggest that the pulsar PSR J1803-2137 near the molecular features may play a role in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray production. The W 31 region exhibits another active star formation, while no <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source is yet known.

articleTitle: Multiband Photopolarimetric Monitoring of an Outburst of the Blazar 3C 454.3 in 2007
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on optical—near-infrared photopolarimetric observations of a blazar 3C 454.3 over 200 d. The object experienced an optical outburst in 2007 July. This outburst was followed by a short state fainter than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V =$</tex> 15.2 mag, lasting <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>25 d. The object then entered an active state during which we observed short flares having a timescale of 3–10 d. The object showed two types of features in the color–magnitude relationship. One was a “bluer-when-brighter” trend in the outburst state, and the other was a “redder-when-brighter” trend in the faint state. These two types of features suggest a contribution of thermal emission to the observed flux, as suspected in previous studies. Our polarimetric observation detected two episodes of rotation of the polarization vector. The first one was a counterclockwise rotation in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$QU$</tex> plane during the outburst state. After this rotation event of the polarization vector, the object entered a rapidly fading stage. The second one was seen in a series of flares during the active state. Each flare had a specific position angle of polarization, which apparently rotated clockwise from the first to the last flares. Thus, the object exhibited rotations of the polarization vector in opposite directions. We estimated a decay timescale of the short flares during the active state, and then calculated an upper limit of the strength of the magnetic field, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B =$</tex> 0.2 G, assuming a typical beaming factor of blazars, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta =$</tex> 20. This upper limit of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex> is smaller than those previously estimated from spectral analysis.

articleTitle: ASTE Simultaneous HCN (4–3) and HCO+(4–3) Observations of the Two Luminous Infrared Galaxies NGC 4418 and Arp 220
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report the results of HCN (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3) and HCO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3) observations of two luminous infrared galaxies, NGC 4418 and Arp 220, made using the Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment (ASTE). The ASTE wide-band correlator provided simultaneous observations of HCN (4–3) and HCO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+}$</tex>(4–3) lines, and a precise determination of their flux ratios. Both galaxies showed high HCN (4–3) to HCO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+}$</tex>(4–3) flux ratios of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>2, possibly due to AGN-related phenomena. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 4–3 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0 transition flux ratios for HCN (HCO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+}$</tex>) are similar to those expected for fully thermalized (sub-thermally excited) gas in both sources, in spite of HCN’s higher critical density. If we assume collisional excitation and neglect an infrared radiative pumping process, our non-LTE analysis suggests that HCN traces gas with significantly higher density than HCO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+}$</tex>. In Arp 220, we separated the double-peaked HCN (4–3) emission into eastern and western nuclei, based on velocity information. We confirmed that the eastern nucleus showed a higher HCN (4–3) to HCN (1–0) flux ratio, and thus contained a larger amount of highly excited molecular gas than the western nucleus.

articleTitle: Photometric Investigation and Possible Light-Time Effect in the Orbital Period of a Marginal Contact System, CW Cassiopeiae
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The first complete charge-coupled device (CCD) light curves in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex> passbands of a neglected contact binary system, CW Cassiopeiae (CW Cas), are presented. They were analyzed simultaneously by using the Wilson and Devinney (WD) code (1971, ApJ, 166, 605). The photometric solution indicates that CW Cas is a W-type W UMa system with a mass ratio of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{2}/m_{1} =$</tex> 2.234, and that it is in a marginal contact state with a contact degree of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 6.5% and a relatively large temperature difference of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 327 K between its two components. Based on the minimum times collected from the literature, together with the new ones obtained in this study, the orbital period changes of CW Cas were investigated in detail. It was found that a periodical variation overlaps with a secular period decrease in its orbital period. The long-term period decrease with a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$dP/dt = -$</tex>3.44 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8} $</tex>d yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> can be interpreted either by mass transfer from the more-massive component to the less-massive with a rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${d}m_{2}/dt = -$</tex>3.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8} M_{\odot} $</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, or by mass and angular-momentum losses through magnetic braking due to a magnetic stellar wind. A low-amplitude cyclic variation with a period of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T =$</tex> 63.7 yr might be caused by the light-time effect due to the presence of a third body.

articleTitle: The Spectral Features of Disk and Corona with Mass Evaporation in the Low/Hard State
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigate the spectral features of accretion flows composed of an outer cool, optically thick disk and inner hot, optically thin, advection dominated accretion flows (ADAF) within the framework of disk and corona with mass evaporation (Liu et al. 2002a, ApJ, 575, 117). In this work, both the magnetic field and Compton scattering of soft photons from the disk by electrons in the corona are included to calculate the evaporation rates at different distances. The disk is truncated at the distance where the evaporation rate equals to the accretion rate [<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot m_{\rm evap}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{\rm tr}$</tex>) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$= \dot m$</tex>]. For a series of accretion rates, the corresponding truncation radii are calculated out, with which we are able to calculate the emergent spectra from the inner ADAF + outer disk + corona. At very low accretion rates, the spectra are similar to that of a pure ADAF because the disk is truncated at large distances. The disk component becomes important at high accretion rates since the truncation occurs at small distances. An anti-correlation between the Eddington ratio, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\xi \equiv L_{0.5-25 \ {\rm keV}}/L_{\rm Edd}$</tex>, and the hard X-ray photon index, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{3-25 \ {\rm keV}}$</tex>, in low/hard states is predicted by the model. Comparing the theoretical results with observations, we find that our model can reproduce the anti-correlation between the Eddington ratio, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\xi$</tex>, and the hard X-ray photon index observed for the X-ray binary XTE J1118+480.

articleTitle: Additional Acceleration of Protons and Energetic Neutrino Production in a Filamentary Jet of the Blazar Markarian 501
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Blazars have been regarded as one of the most powerful sources of the highest energy cosmic rays and also their byproducts, neutrinos. Provided that a magnetized filamentary system is established in a blazar jet as well, we could apply the mechanism of multi-stage diffusive shock acceleration to a feasible TeV emitter, Mrk 501 to evaluate the achievable maximum energy of protons. Taking conceivable energy restriction into account systematically, it seems adequate to say that EeV-protons are produced at this site by our present model. We also estimate neutrino fluxes generated by these accelerated protons, and discuss the detectability based on an updated kilometer-scale telescope, such as IceCube.

articleTitle: Internal Fine Structure of Ellerman Bombs
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted coordinated observations of Ellerman bombs (EBs) between Hinode Satellite and Hida Observatory (HOP12). Ca II H broad-band filter images of NOAA 10966 on 2007 August 9 and 10 were obtained with the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) aboard the Hinode Satellite, and many bright points were observed. We identified a total of 4 bright points as EBs, and studied the temporal variation of their morphological fine structures and spectroscopic characteristics. With high-resolution Ca II H images of SOT, we found that the EBs, thus far thought of as single bright features, are composed of a few of fine subcomponents. Also, by using Stokes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I$</tex>/<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex> filtergrams with Hinode/SOT, and Ca II H spectroheliograms with Hida/Domeless Solar Telescope (DST), our observation showed: (1) The mean duration, the mean width, the mean length, and the mean aspect ratio of the subcomponents were 390 s, 170 km, 450 km, and 2.7, respectively. (2) Subcomponents started to appear on the magnetic neutral lines, and extended their lengths from the original locations. (3) When the Ca II H line of EBs showed the characteristic blue asymmetry, they are associated with the appearance or re-brightening of subcomponents. Summarizing our results, we obtained an observational view that elementary magnetic reconnections take place one by one successively and intermittently in EBs, and that their manifestation is the fine subcomponents of the EB phenomena.

articleTitle: Bright X-Ray Flares from the BL Lac Object Markarian 421, Detected with MAXI in 2010 January and February
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Strong X-ray flares from the blazar Mrk 421 were detected in 2010 January and February through 7-month monitoring with the MAXI GSC. The maximum 2–10 keV flux in the January and February flares was measured to be 120<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>10 mCrab and 164<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>17 mCrab, respectively; the latter is the highest among those reported from the object. A comparison of the MAXI and Swift BAT data suggests a convex X-ray spectrum with an approximated photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex> 2. This spectrum is consistent with a picture that MAXI is observing near the synchrotron peak frequency. The source exhibited a spectral variation during these flares, slightly different from those in previous observations, in which the positive correlation between the flux and hardness was widely reported. By equating the halving decay timescale in the January flare, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_{ m d}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 2.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{4}\ $</tex>s, to the synchrotron cooling time, the magnetic field was evaluated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 4.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>G (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta/$</tex>10)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/3}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta$</tex> is the jet beaming factor. Assuming that the light crossing time of the emission region is shorter than the doubling rise time, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_{ m r}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{4}\ $</tex>s, the region size was roughly estimated as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex>< 6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{15}\ $</tex>cm (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta/$</tex>10). These results are consistent with values previously reported. For the February flare, the rise time, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_{ m r}$</tex>< 1.3 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5}\ $</tex>s, gives a loose upper limit on the size as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex>< 4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{16}\ $</tex>cm <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\delta/10)$</tex>, although the longer decay time, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_{ m d}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5}\ $</tex>s, indicates <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 1.5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta/$</tex>10)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/3}$</tex>, which is weaker than the previous results. This could be reconciled by invoking a scenario that this flare is a superposition of unresolved events with a shorter timescale.

articleTitle: Thermal and Magnetic Parameters in Solar Flares Derived from GOES X-Ray Light Curves
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The purpose of this study is to reproduce the GOES X-ray (1–8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\AA}$</tex>) light curves of the impulsive phase of 20 solar flares and to estimate the thermal and magnetic parameters in flare loops. The expected X-ray light curves are calculated from the values of the coronal field strength and inflow velocity under some assumptions. We used the magnetic reconnection heating model of Shibata and Yokoyama (2002, ApJ, 577, 422), photospheric vector magnetic field data, and a simple 1-D flare loop model. It is found the maximum inflow velocities are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{7} $</tex>cm s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and that the maximum magnetic reconnection rates are 0.006–0.9, and further that the characteristic coronal field strengths are 6–100 G. Using the thermal and magnetic parameters derived, we found that geometrically our calculated flare loops are higher than the potential fields that model the postflare loops, and are also higher than the preflare loops containing magnetic free energy that is large enough to provide the thermal energy of a flare. Hence, we conclude that the plasma <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta $</tex> value would be near unity in the flare loops we studied, and the magnetic field lines shrunk during the decay phase. The downward velocities of the field-line shrinkage are estimated to be 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{6}$</tex>–10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{7} $</tex>cm s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> except one event. The height of the reconnection point was roughly estimated to be from 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10} $</tex>cm to 4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10} $</tex>cm. We propose a new interpretation of the Neupert effect, and also discuss a temporal relationship between the X-ray flux and the flare loop heating.

articleTitle: Modeling the Gamma-Ray Emission Produced by Runaway Cosmic Rays in the Environment of RX J1713.7$-$3946
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Diffusive shock acceleration in supernova remnants is the most widely invoked paradigm to explain the Galactic cosmic ray spectrum. Cosmic rays escaping from supernova remnants diffuse into the interstellar medium and collide with the ambient atomic and molecular gas. From such collisions gamma-rays are created, which can possibly provide the first evidence of a parent population of runaway cosmic rays. We present model predictions for the GeV to TeV gamma-ray emission produced by the collisions of runaway cosmic rays with the gas in the surroundings of the shell-type supernova remnant RX J1713.7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>3946. The spectral and spatial distributions of the emission, which depend upon the source age, the source injection history, the diffusion regime, and the distribution of the ambient gas, as mapped by the LAB and NANTEN surveys, are studied in detail. For the surrounding region of RX J1713<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>3946 in particular, we find out that it depends on the energy band one is observing whether one may observe startlingly different spectra or may not detect any enhanced emission with respect to the diffuse emission contributed by background cosmic rays. This result has important implications for current and future gamma-ray experiments.

articleTitle: Observations of Chromospheric Anemone Jets with Hinode Ca II Broadband Filtergraph and Hida Ca II Spectroheliograph
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the first simultaneous observations of chromospheric “anemone” jets in solar active regions with the Hinode Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) Ca II H broadband filtergraph and the Ca II K spetroheliograph on the Domeless Solar Telescope (DST) at Hida Observatory. During the period of coordinated observations, nine chromospheric anemone jets were simultaneously observed with the two instruments. These observations revealed three important features: (1) the jets are generated in the lower chromosphere; i.e., these cannot be seen in Ca II K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex>; (2) the length and lifetime of the jets are 0.4–5 Mm and 40–320 s, respectively; (3) the apparent velocity of the jets observed with the SOT is 3–24 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, while the Ca II K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{3}$</tex> component at the jets shows a blueshift (in 5 events) in the range of 2–6 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The chromospheric anemone jets are associated with mixed polarity regions, which are either small emerging flux regions or moving magnetic features. It is found that the Ca II K line often shows red or blue asymmetry in the K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{2}$</tex>/K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{1}$</tex> component; the footpoint of the jets associated with emerging flux regions often shows a redshift (2–16 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>), while the one with moving magnetic features shows a blueshift (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>5 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>). A detailed analysis of the magnetic evolution of the jet-forming regions revealed that the reconnection rate (or canceling rate) of the total magnetic flux at the footpoint of the jets is on the order of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{16}\ $</tex>Mx s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and the resulting magnetic energy release rate is (1.1–10) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{24}\ $</tex>erg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, with a total energy release of (1–13) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{26}\ $</tex>erg for the duration of the magnetic cancellation, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>130 s. These are comparable to the estimated total energy, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{26}\ $</tex>erg, in a single chromospheric anemone jet. In addition to the DST Ca II K spectroheliogram and the SOT Ca II H broadband filtergram, we also used for analysis an SOT magnetogram as well as a Hida H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> filtergram. We present a physical model of the jet based on the observation, and discuss the relation between chromospheric anemone jets and Ellerman bombs.

articleTitle: Search for Outer Massive Bodies around Transiting Planetary Systems: Candidates of Faint Stellar Companions around HAT-P-7
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present results of direct imaging observations for HAT-P-7 taken with the Subaru HiCIAO and the Calar Alto AstraLux. Since the close-in transiting planet HAT-P-7b was reported to have a highly tilted orbit, massive bodies such as giant planets, brown dwarfs, and a binary star are expected to exist in the outer region of this system. We show that there are indeed two candidates for distant faint stellar companions around HAT-P-7. We discuss how such companions can play a role on the orbital evolution of HAT-P-7b. We conclude that since there is a third body in the system, as reported by Winn et al. (2009, ApJ, 763, L99), Kozai migration is less likely, while planet–planet scattering is possible.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of the Great Annihilator and the Surrounding Diffuse Emissions
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report the Suzaku observations of 1E 1740.7-2942, a black hole candidate called the “Great Annihilator” (GA). The high-quality spectrum of Suzaku provides the severest constraints on the parameters of the GA. Two clumpy structures are found around the GA in the line images of FeI K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> at 6.4 keV and SXV K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> at 2.45 keV. One clump, named M 359.23-0.04, exhibits the 6.4-keV line with an equivalent width of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>1.2 keV, and is associated with a molecular cloud in the radio CS (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J =$</tex> 1–0) map. Thus, the 6.4-keV line from M 359.23-0.04 is likely due to X-ray fluorescence irradiated by an external X-ray source. The irradiating X-rays would be either a past flare of Sagittarius A<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\ast$</tex> or a bright nearby source, the GA. The other clump, named G 359.12-0.05, is associated with the radio supernova remnant candidate G 359.07-0.02. We therefore propose that G 359.12-0.05 is an X-ray counterpart of G 359.07-0.02. G 359.12-0.05 has a thin thermal plasma spectrum with a temperature of kT<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex> 0.9 keV. The plasma parameters of G 359.12-0.05 are consistent with those of a single supernova remnant in the Galactic center region.

articleTitle: Solar Eclipses in the First Half of the Chunqiu Period
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In the Chinese chronicle Chunqiu, which describes a partial (722 BC–481 BC) history of the Chunqiu Period (770 BC–403 BC), there are recorded 37 solar eclipse observations, starting in 720 BC and ending in 481 BC. Among these, there are 10 eclipse records that lack either the cyclic day number or a statement of ‘the new moon’, or both. Three explanatory books Zuoshi-Zhuan, Guliang-Zhuan, and Gongyang-Zhuan written in the Zhanguo Period (403 BC–221 BC) have different interpretations concerning these records. Zuoshi-Zhuan simply says that royal astronomers forgot to record these data. On the other hand, Guliang-Zhuan says that these eclipses were observed on the last day of the month or during the night. Gongyang-Zhuan says that these were mainly observed on the second day of the month. A famous astronomer, Liuxin in the Han Dynasty, argued close to the idea of Gongyang-Zhuan. These discussions are related to the problem of establishing a precise calendar system in the Chunqiu Period. Controversial arguments continue until today. A Japanese astronomer, Toshio Watanabe (1958), conjectured that these eclipses may have been observed at sunrise or sunset. In the present report, we intend to confirm Watanabe’s conjecture, and after confirming this we use this property to accurately determine the range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta T$</tex> (see section 1 for definition) in this period. We have obtained new <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta T$</tex> ranges in seconds from five eclipses which accompanied deep contemporaneous solar eclipses.

articleTitle: Probing the Peculiar Behavior of GRS 1915+105 at Near-Eddington Luminosity
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: To understand the nature of supercritical accretion, we systematically analyzed the RXTE/PCA data of GRS 1915+105 in its quasi-steady states, by choosing data with small variability during 1999–2000. We applied a multicolor disk plus a thermal Comptonization model, and took into consideration accurate interstellar absorption, a reflection component (with an iron-K emission line), and absorption features from the disk wind self-consistently. The total luminosity ranges from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>0.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm E}$</tex> to slightly above <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm E}$</tex>. There is a strong correlation between the inner disk temperature and the fraction of the disk component. Most of the Comptonization-dominated (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>50% total flux) spectra show <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm in} \sim $</tex> 1 keV with a high electron temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex>10 keV, which may correspond to the very high state in canonical black hole X-ray binaries (BHBs). In contrast, the disk-dominated spectra have <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm in} \sim $</tex> 2 keV with a low temperature (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex>10 keV) and optically thick Comptonization, and show two separate branches in the luminosity vs. innermost temperature (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm in}$</tex>) diagram. The lower branch clearly follows the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L \propto T_{\rm in}^4$</tex>-track. Furthermore, by applying the extended disk blackbody (or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p$</tex>-free disk) model, we found that 9 out of 12 datasets with disk luminosity above 0.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm E}$</tex> prefer a flatter temperature gradient than that in the standard disk (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p <$</tex> 0.7). We interpret that, in the lower branch, the disk extends down to the innermost stable circular orbit, and the source is most probably in the slim-disk state. A rapidly spinning black hole can explain both the lack of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L \propto T_{\rm in}^2$</tex>-track and a high value of the spectral hardening factor (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim $</tex>4) that would be required for a non-rotating black hole. The spectra in the upper branch are consistent with the picture of a truncated disk with low-temperature Comptonization. This state was uniquely observed from GRS 1915+105 among BHBs, which may be present at near-Eddington luminosity.

articleTitle: Spitzer Space Telescope Constraint on the Stellar Mass of a z = 6.96 Lyα Emitter
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We obtained mid-infrared 3.6 and 4.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \mu$</tex>m imaging of a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z =$</tex> 6.96 Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitter (LAE), IOK-1, discovered in the Subaru Deep Field, using Spitzer Space Telescope Infrared Array Camera observations. After removal of a nearby bright source, we found that IOK-1 is not significantly detected in any of these infrared bands to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{3.6\mu{\rm m}} \sim$</tex> 24.00 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{4.5\mu{\rm m}} \sim$</tex> 23.54 at 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex>. Fitting population synthesis models to the spectral energy distribution consisting of the upper limit fluxes of the optical-to-infrared non-detection images and fluxes in detection images, we constrained the stellar mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\ast$</tex>, of IOK-1. This LAE could have either a mass as low as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\ast \lesssim$</tex> 2–9 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{8}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> for young age (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex>10 Myr) and low dust reddening (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_V \sim$</tex> 0) or a mass as large as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_\ast \lesssim$</tex> 1–4 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}\ M_{\odot}$</tex> for either old age (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ > \ $</tex>100 Myr) or high dust reddening (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_V \sim$</tex> 1.5). This would be within the range of masses of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim$</tex> 3–6.6 LAEs studied to date, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^6$</tex>–10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{10}\ M_{\odot}$</tex>. Hence, IOK-1 is not a particularly unique galaxy with extremely high mass or low mass, but is similar to one of the LAEs seen at later epochs.

articleTitle: Metallicity of the Fossil Group NGC 1550 Observed with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We studied the temperature and metal abundance distributions of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) in a group of galaxies, NGC 1550, observed with Suzaku. NGC 1550 is classified as a fossil group, which has few bright member galaxies, except for the central galaxy. Thus, such a type of galaxy is important to investigate how metals are enriched to the ICM. With the Suzaku XIS instrument, we directly measured not only the Si, S, and Fe lines, but also the O and Mg lines, and obtained those abundances to an outer region of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>0.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{180}$</tex> for the first time, and confirmed that the metals in the ICM of such a fossil group are indeed extending to a large radius. We found steeper gradients for the Mg, Si, S, and Fe abundances, while O showed an almost flat abundance distribution. Abundance ratios of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>-elements to Fe were similar to those of the other groups and poor clusters. We calculated the number ratio of type II to type Ia supernovae for the ICM enrichment to be 2.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \pm\ $</tex>0.5 within 0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{180}$</tex>; the value is consistent with those for the other groups and poor clusters observed with Suzaku. We also calculated the metal mass-to-light ratios (MLRs) for Fe, O, and Mg with the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex>-band and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>-band luminosities of the member galaxies of NGC 1550. The derived MLRs are comparable to those of the NGC 5044 group in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex>< 0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{180}$</tex> region, while those of NGC 1550 are slightly higher than those of NGC 5044 in the outer region.

articleTitle: Prospects for a Very High-Energy Blazar Survey by the Next-Generation Cherenkov Telescopes
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The prospects for future blazar surveys by next-generation very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray telescopes, such as Advanced Gamma-ray Imaging System (AGIS) and Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), are investigated using the latest model of blazar luminosity function and its evolution, which is in good agreement with the flux and redshift distribution of observed blazars as well as the extragalactic gamma-ray background. We extend and improve the template of spectral energy distributions (SEDs) based on the blazar SED sequence paradigm, to make it reliable also in the VHE bands (above 100 GeV) by comparing with the existing VHE blazar data. Assuming the planned CTA sensitivities, a blind survey using a total survey time of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>100 hr could detect <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\ $</tex>3 VHE blazars, with larger expected numbers for wider/shallower surveys. We also discuss a following-up of Fermi blazars. The detectability of VHE blazars in the plane of the Fermi flux and redshift is presented, which would be useful for future survey planning. Prospects and strategies are discussed to constrain the extragalactic background light (EBL) by using the absorption feature of brightest blazar spectra, as well as cut-offs in the redshift distribution. We will be able to get useful constraints on EBL by VHE blazars at different redshifts ranging 0.3–1 TeV corresponding to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z =$</tex> 0.10–0.36.

articleTitle: Study of the Intracluster and Intergalactic Medium in the Sculptor Supercluster with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We studied the high-temperature plasma in the direction of the Sculptor supercluster at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z =$</tex> 0.108 with Suzaku. Suzaku carried out four observations in the supercluster: namely, A 2811, A 2811 offset, A 2804, A 2801 regions in 2005 November–December, including the regions beyond the virial radii of these clusters. The spectra taken in regions outside of the virial radii of the member clusters were used as background that included both of the Galactic and Cosmic X-ray Background (CXB) components. Temperature and metal abundance profiles were determined to the virial radii of the member clusters, and we then searched for oxygen line emission in the region outside of the virial radii of the clusters. As a result, the temperature of the clusters decreased toward the virial radii, and the spectral fits for the filament region did not require any extra component other than the Galactic and CXB components. We constrained the intensities of the OVII and OVIII lines to be less than 8.1 and 5.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-8}$</tex> photons cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}\ $</tex>arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}\ $</tex>, respectively, as 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ \sigma$</tex> upper limits in the filament region. The intensity of OVII indicates <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H}$</tex>< 1.6 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-5}\ $</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Z/$</tex>0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ Z_{\odot}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L/$</tex>25 Mpc)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex>, which corresponds to an over density of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta$</tex>< 60(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Z/$</tex>0.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ Z_{\odot}$</tex>)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L/$</tex>25 Mpc)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1/2}$</tex>.

Author Keywords: galaxies: clusters: individual (A 2801, A 2804, and A 2811)

articleTitle: Transiting Extrasolar Planet with a Companion: Effects of Orbital Eccentricity and Inclination
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Continuing work initiated in an earlier publication (Sato & Asada, 2009, PASJ, 61, L29), we consider light curves influenced by the orbital inclination and eccentricity of a companion in orbit around a transiting extrasolar planet (in a planet–satellite system or a hypothetical true binary). We show that the semimajor axis, eccentricity and inclination angle of a ‘moon’ orbit around the host planet can be determined by the transit method alone. For this purpose, we present a formulation for the parameter determinations in a small-eccentricity approximation as well as in the exact form. As a result, the semimajor axis is expressed in terms of observables, such as brightness changes, transit durations and intervals in light curves. We also discuss a narrow region of parameters that produce a mutual transit by an extrasolar satellite.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of the Anomalous X-Ray Pulsar 1E 1841−045
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the results of a Suzaku observation of the anomalous X-ray pulsar (AXP) 1E 1841<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>045 at the center of the supernova remnant Kes 73. We confirmed that the energy-dependent spectral models obtained by previous separate observations were also satisfied over a wide energy range from 0.4 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>70 keV, simultaneously. Here, the models below <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>10 keV were a combination of blackbody (BB) and power-law (PL) functions, or of two BBs with different temperatures at 0.6–7.0 keV (Morii et al. 2003, PASJ, 55, L45), and that above <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20 keV was a PL function (Kuiper et al. 2004, ApJ, 613, 1173). The combination BB <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> PL <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> PL was found to best represent the phase-averaged spectrum. Phase-resolved spectroscopy indicated the existence of two emission regions, one with a thermal and the other with a non-thermal nature. The combination BB <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> BB <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex> PL was also found to represent the phase-averaged spectrum well. However, we found that this model is physically unacceptable due to an excessively large area of the emission region of the blackbody. Nonetheless, we found that the temperatures and radii of the two blackbody components showed moderate correlations in the phase-resolved spectra. The fact that the same correlations have been observed between the phase-averaged spectra of various magnetars (Nakagawa et al. 2009, PASJ, 61, 109) suggests that a self-similar function can approximate the intrinsic energy spectra of magnetars below <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>10 keV.

articleTitle: Bayesian Approach to Find a Long-Term Trend in Erratic Polarization Variations Observed in Blazars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We developed a method of separating a long-term trend from observed temporal variations of polarization in blazars using a Bayesian approach. The temporal variation of the polarization vector is apparently erratic in most blazars, while several objects have occasionally exhibited systematic variations, for example an increase of the polarization degree associated with a flare of the total flux. We assume that the observed polarization vector is a superposition of two distinct components: a long-term trend and a short-term variation component responsible for short flares. Our Bayesian model estimates a long-term trend that satisfies the condition that the total flux correlates with the polarized flux of the short-term component. We demonstrate that assumed long-term polarization components are successfully separated by the Bayesian model for artificial data. We applied this method to the three photopolarimetric data of OJ 287, S5 0716+714, and S2 0109+224. Simple and systematic long-term trends were obtained in OJ 287 and S2 0109+224, while no such trend was confirmed in S5 0716+714. We propose that the apparently erratic variations of polarization in OJ 287 and S2 0109+224 are due to the presence of the long-term polarization component. The behavior of polarization in S5 0716+714 during the period of observation implies the presence of a number of polarization components showing variations on a quite short time-scale.

articleTitle: Possible Origins of Dispersion of the Peak Energy–Brightness Correlations of Gamma-Ray Bursts
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We collected and reanalyzed about 200 GRB data of prompt-emission with known redshift observed until the end of 2009, and selected 101 GRBs that were well-observed to have good spectral parameters in order to determine the spectral peak energy (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex>), 1-second peak luminosity (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm p}$</tex>) and isotropic energy (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm iso}$</tex>). Using our newly constructed database with 101 GRBs, we first revised the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm p}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm iso}$</tex> correlations. The correlation coefficients of the revised correlations were 0.889 for 99 degrees of freedom for the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm p}$</tex> correlation and 0.867 for 96 degrees of freedom for the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm iso}$</tex> correlation.
